content.text: do we have an allowed_domain list or some? show me
I’m using the i-have-adhd skill. I’ll check the code for domain allowlists and show you where they’re defined.

**Yes. We have `allowed_domains` for each login connection.** It’s generated from that account’s website:

```python
allowed_domains=[urlsplit(origin).hostname]
```

For example, `https://github.com` produces `["github.com"]`. See [managed_auth.py:762](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/managed_auth.py:762).

There’s also a fixed list for validating **Kernel-hosted login links**:

```python
{
    "auth.kernel.com",
    "auth.kernel.sh",
    "auth.onkernel.com",
    "managed-auth.onkernel.com",
}
```

See [kernel_auth_client.py:28](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/kernel_auth_client.py:28).

**I found no global website allowlist restricting ordinary browsing in our runtime/config.**
It’s meant to keep a login flow scoped to the intended website. I’ll check Kernel’s definition so I can explain exactly what it restricts.

**They protect where credentials are entered and which login links we trust.**

- **`allowed_domains`** limits where Kernel may enter credentials during login. A redirect to an unrelated site shouldn’t receive your password. Kernel says omitting this field leaves credential entry unrestricted by the primary domain. Common sign-in providers such as Google and Microsoft are automatically allowed. [Kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/ai-library/agent-identity-how-to-authenticate-an-ai-browser-agent#implementing-the-pattern-with-kernels-managed-auth)
- **`_HOSTED_HOSTS`** makes our backend reject hosted login links pointing outside the listed Kernel domains. That helps prevent us from passing you an unexpected credential-collection URL. [Our validation code](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/kernel_auth_client.py:88)

One clarification to my earlier answer: the single hostname we send **isn’t the complete effective list**, because Kernel also permits those common sign-in providers. These checks protect authentication; they don’t impose a global browsing allowlist.
so how's our security posture in that sense?
The domain checks are useful, but they cover only part of credential security. I’ll check how we enforce them across login redirects, saved credentials, and browser access.

content.text: The current code now explicitly allows `accounts.google.com` for a small set of Google apps, and rejects unexpected additions to a connection’s domain list. The larger limit is that credential protections don’t stop an authenticated agent from reading sensitive data or taking unwanted actions. I’m checking the relevant tests and browser controls.

All 203 targeted authentication tests passed. Kernel’s documented policy is broader than an exact hostname: it also permits subdomains and built-in sign-in providers. I also found a validation-order gap worth checking: we start a newly created login before checking all of the returned security settings.

content.text:
**We have meaningful credential protections, but incomplete protection against a malicious page steering an authenticated agent.** I also found one concrete hardening gap.

| Area | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Saved credentials** | Login fills check the saved website origin and active page. Browser access also checks account and session ownership. |
| **Hosted login links** | Strict HTTPS and exact Kernel-host checks reject lookalike domains and malformed links. |
| **Effective domain scope** | Broader than the list suggests: Kernel permits subdomains and built-in sign-in providers. These are provider-enforced rules. [Kernel specification](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/api-reference/managed-auth/create-auth-connection#body-allowed-domains) |
| **Data after login** | The login allowlist doesn’t prevent the agent from reading private content and sending it elsewhere. Personal-information fills also lack the saved credential’s fixed destination restriction. [Personal-data boundary](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/kernel_service.py:591) |

**The confirmed gap:** we start a newly created login before fully checking its returned domain policy. In an isolated reproduction, a fake response containing an extra attacker domain still triggered login; our later check rejected it. That demonstrates a validation-order bug, **not an observed credential leak**. [Dispatch code](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/managed_auth.py:778)

My first hardening priority would be to **validate the complete connection policy before starting login**. The larger security priority is controlling where sensitive data may go after authentication.

**Verified locally:** 203 targeted authentication tests passed, plus the isolated reproduction above. Live deployment and malicious-site resistance were not verified in this review.
